<a id="Libpetri-Spec-CONC_024"></a>
## CONC-024: Precomputed Timing Arrays

`Libpetri.Spec.CONC_024` · Kind **F** · Scope the precompiled net of every implementation · Source **verbatim** (spec/05-concurrency.md) · Sign-off **pending** · Statement hash `853131f1a329c165`

| Natural language | Plain reading | Lean statement |
|---|---|---|
| *When* a net is precompiled, the timing arrays *shall* hold, for each transition, the `earliest()` of its timing in the array's unit and the `hasDeadline()` of its timing ([TIME-001]).<br><br>*When* a net is precompiled, the timing arrays *shall* hold, for each transition whose timing's `hasDeadline()` is true, the `latest()` of its timing in the array's unit.<br><br>*When* a net is precompiled, `allImmediate` *shall* be true exactly when every transition of the net has the timing `Immediate`.<br><br>*When* a net is precompiled, `anyDeadlines` *shall* be true exactly when some transition of the net has a timing whose `hasDeadline()` is true. | 1. For every timing contract K (the accessors of TIME-001) and every net of n transitions whose timings, by transition id, are tm:<br>2. for every transition id i below n, the earliest entry is K's earliest() of tm i (in K's unit, milliseconds) and the deadline flag is K's hasDeadline() of tm i;<br>3. for every transition id i below n with K's hasDeadline() of tm i true, the latest entry is K's latest() of tm i (in K's unit);<br>4. allImmediate is true exactly when tm i is Immediate for every i below n;<br>5. anyDeadlines is true exactly when K's hasDeadline() of tm i is true for some i below n. | <pre>fun K C ↦<br>  ∀ (n : ℕ) (tm : ℕ → Novel.TimedScg.Timing),<br>    (∀ i &lt; n,<br>        (C n tm).earliest i = K.earliest (tm i) ∧<br>          (C n tm).hasDeadline i = K.hasDeadline (tm i)) ∧<br>      (∀ i &lt; n, K.hasDeadline (tm i) = true → (C n tm).latest i = K.latest (tm i)) ∧<br>        ((C n tm).allImmediate = true ↔ ∀ i &lt; n, tm i = Novel.TimedScg.Timing.immediate) ∧<br>          ((C n tm).anyDeadlines = true ↔ ∃ i &lt; n, K.hasDeadline (tm i) = true)</pre> |

**Assumptions**

- A timing compiler maps the number n of a net's transitions and the timing of each transition, by declaration index (the transition id of the precompiled net), to a timing table: an earliest entry, a latest entry and a deadline flag per transition id, and the two global flags. Entries at an id of n or more are not read and no line constrains them. Timing, enablement and the marking at run time play no part: the table is a function of the timings alone.
- The entries are stated through the accessors of a timing contract K of TIME-001, not through Timing.earliest directly: this block says the table holds what the accessors return, TIME-001 says what they return. A joint model satisfies TIME_001 K and CONC_024 K C with the same K, and conc024_skipDeadlines needs both. Bounds are naturals in milliseconds, as in TIME-001.
- The bullet list names a nanosecond and a millisecond array for each bound, and the body sentence 'Millisecond arrays are precomputed to avoid nanosecond-to-millisecond division on the hot path.' and AC4 (the millisecond values match the nanosecond values within rounding) concern that pair. Only Java keeps both units; Rust and TypeScript keep milliseconds only (clash conc-b#7). The block states one entry per bound in the contract's unit (milliseconds), which is what the quoted sentences mean by 'in the array's unit': Java's earliestNanos[] holds earliest() converted to nanoseconds, its earliestMillis[] the same bound in milliseconds. The unit pair and AC4 are a layout property of the Java runtime (Q) and no line encodes them; the wording that makes the bullet list unit-neutral waits for ruling D20, and until then those bullets, the body sentence and AC4 stay normative prose that only Java meets.
- 'MAX_VALUE if no deadline' is not encoded: no line constrains the latest entry of a transition whose deadline flag is clear, and conc024_noDeadlineLatest_free shows the block accepts any value there, 0 included (a compiler that zero-fills the array and writes only flagged entries, so delayed(5) gets the entries 5 and 0). The runtimes store three different values there (Java Long.MAX_VALUE, Rust f64::MAX, TypeScript the maximum duration, which is latest() of Immediate and Delayed). Each reads the entry only behind the flag: Rust precompiled_backend.rs:1033 and :1395, Java PrecompiledNetExecutor.java:2123 and :2790, TypeScript precompiled-net-executor.ts:839 and :1723. conc024_deadlineAt proves that such a flag-guarded read is the same under every compiler that satisfies CONC-024, so the free entry changes nothing a guarded reader sees. A fifth line 'the latest entry without the flag is no smaller than latest()' would hold of the three runtimes, but it would settle the D20 item (clash conc-b#7, whose recommendation is that the entry is meaningful only where the flag is set) ahead of the ruling, so it stays out; if D20 keeps a fixed value, that line is added and conc024_maxValueCompile 0 becomes its forbids evidence.
- The deadline flag is hasDeadline() by variant (ruling D2, TIME-001 line 3): Exact has the flag although it is enforced softly and never reaped (TIME-006, TIME-013). A flag read off the bounds (latest below the maximum duration) is killed as CONC_024_forbids_latestBelowMax on window(0, maximum). The separate Exact flag every runtime keeps is not in the spec's list and is not encoded.
- AC1 (populated at compile time, not computed per cycle) and the purpose 'to avoid virtual dispatch on timing types during execution' are cost and layout (Q), and no line encodes them. That a compiler is a function of n and the timings alone is the model's typing, not a checked property: it cannot tell a runtime that fills the table once from one that refills it every cycle.
- Line 3 tests the variant (tm i is Immediate) while lines 1, 2 and 4 go through K, because the quoted sentence names the variant `Immediate` and the contract has no accessor for it. The two bases agree in a joint model: conc024_flags_exclusive proves that under TIME_001 K the flags allImmediate and anyDeadlines are never both set.
- The bullets 'true if all transitions are immediate' and 'true if any transition has a deadline' state only the direction that makes the flag set; the quoted 'exactly when' sentences add the converse and fix the reading of 'immediate' as the variant (so delayed(0) does not count). The bullets themselves are left as written: rewording them is a D20 item. Both directions are killed when violated: the unsafe one by CONC_024_forbids_earliestZero, CONC_024_forbids_noDeadlineImmediate and CONC_024_mutant_reapable, the conservative one (allImmediate stuck false, anyDeadlines stuck true) by CONC_024_forbids_neverImmediate, CONC_024_forbids_alwaysDeadlines and CONC_024_mutant_safeDirection.
- AC2 (allImmediate allows skipping timing checks entirely for immediate-only nets) is line 3, and conc024_skipTiming shows why the skip is sound: when the flag is set, every transition of the net is Ready exactly when it is Armed, so the checks of the earliest and the latest bound decide nothing. The flag read off the earliest bounds (a Deadline net then skips its deadline) is killed as CONC_024_mutant_earliestZero; the flag read as 'no deadlines' (a Delayed net then fires before its earliest bound) as CONC_024_forbids_noDeadlineImmediate.
- AC3 (anyDeadlines allows skipping deadline enforcement when no deadlines exist) is line 4, and conc024_skipDeadlines shows why the skip is sound: with TIME-001's accessors, when the flag is clear no transition of the net is reapable, so none is ever Expired and enforcement reaps nothing. The flag read as 'some transition is reapable', which ignores Exact, is killed as CONC_024_mutant_reapable: it would reap the same transitions, but the text (hasDeadline() is true for Exact, D2) and the three runtimes count Exact.
- Where a runtime takes the all-immediate fast path, it tests allImmediate together with a single priority level, which is EXEC-002's fast-path condition ReadyIn.FastPath (conc024_fastPath). The link states the condition only; what the fast path does is EXEC-002's subject (ruling D14, open), and the link does not depend on it.
- The test derivation (compile nets with various timing configurations, verify array values and global flags) is CONC_024_nonvacuous: a net with one transition of each variant, a net of Exact transitions only, an all-Immediate net and the empty net.
- The scope is the five variants of the spec (Novel.TimedScg.Timing). Java's deprecated sixth variant Unconstrained, which Java's allImmediate counts as immediate, is not in the spec and not modelled.

<a id="Libpetri-Spec-CONC_025"></a>
## CONC-025: Lazy Marking Synchronization

`Libpetri.Spec.CONC_025` · Kind **B** · Scope precompiled executor · Source **verbatim** (spec/05-concurrency.md) · Sign-off **pending** · Statement hash `96aba68ca43382fb`

| Natural language | Plain reading | Lean statement |
|---|---|---|
| The materialized Marking accurately reflects the current ring buffer state.<br><br>*When* the executor materializes a Marking, it *shall* give each place the token storage holds a queue for exactly the tokens of that queue at that moment, in queue order. | 1. For every executor X over the token store S:<br>2. at every state that zero or more steps reach from a state a run starts from, the start state included, the materialised marking gives each place S holds a queue for exactly the queue S holds for it, oldest first. | <pre>fun S X ↦<br>  ∀ (s₀ s : X.σ),<br>    X.init s₀ →<br>      Relation.ReflTransGen X.step s₀ s →<br>        ∀ (p : PlaceId), S.ok (X.store s) p → X.mat s p = S.view (X.store s) p</pre> |

**Assumptions**

- The executor is a Materialiser over the store interface MarkingOps of CONC-022 (glossary: Queue order): a state type, the states a run starts from (init: the executor is built and its store loaded from the initial marking, before any cycle), a step relation, the token store inside a state and the marking materialised at a state. A ring buffer is read as the store's queue for a place, S.view, and 'a place that has a ring buffer' (AC3), which the EARS sentence words as 'each place the token storage holds a queue for' in CONC-022's vocabulary, as S.ok. The witness store is refRingStore, the ring pool Libpetri.Pool. The TypeScript precompiled executor keeps a plain array per place instead of a ring (clash conc-b#5, typescript/src/runtime/precompiled-net-executor.ts:179); the statement is over the store interface, so it reads an array store alike. The words 'ring buffer' stay only in the AC3 quote until ruling D20, which would move them to an implementation note.
- The fields describe the executor; they are not chosen to suit the line. init holds of every state a run can start from, store is the token storage the firings consume from and deposit to, and step is every move between two moments at which a marking can be asked for. A description with no start state, with steps that skip such a moment, or with a store field that names a copy the firings never touch says nothing about the executor, as for every abstract relation a requirement block is stated over. Under that reading the snapshot hazard is caught: an executor that materialises from a copy of its rings taken at the start is rejected once store is its live storage (CONC_025_forbids_snapshot).
- 'Current' and 'at that moment' are read as: at a start state and at every state steps reach from it (Relation.ReflTransGen, whose reflexive case is the start state). So a materialisation asked for before the first cycle is constrained (CONC_025_forbids_earlyCache: a cache built before the store is loaded hands out nothing), and an executor that is wrong from the start is rejected there (CONC_025_forbids_seeded hands out every initial token twice, at every state it reaches). A store changed by something other than a step, such as the restore of a snapshot ([CORE-073]), starts a new run, so the state after it is a start state. The line does not require agreement at a state no run reaches: an honest cache whose stale states are unreachable satisfies it.
- A step has the granularity at which a marking can be asked for. AC2's occasions include event emission ([EVT-014]), which the shipped executors do after each firing inside a cycle, so a step is one firing as well as one whole cycle. An executor that refreshes its marking only at the end of a cycle hands out a stale marking between two firings and is rejected (CONC_025_forbids_cycleRefresh). The step relation is abstract, so the line constrains no firing rule and needs no fragment limit: it holds or fails of one executor, timed or not. The reference steps are pcCycle and pcFire, the untimed immediate synchronous cycle of Refinement/Model.lean and one firing in it, but the reference satisfies the line whatever its steps do, because it materialises by reading the store, at every state (CONC_025_reference). A step relation of the executor model RefExec (W5) can be checked against the same statement.
- The holds proof is definitional: the reference's mat is S.view composed with its store field, so CONC_025_reference is rfl at every state, reached or not, and by itself says nothing about the steps. The behavioural content, that the store the reference reads is the one its firings change and that its materialised marking agrees with the bitmap executor's after any number of cycles, is conc025_matches_bitmap (cited, marking_agreement). Tying the Materialiser's step on its store to the queue firing relation of the joint model, so that store cannot be a copy the firings never touch, is a W5 item for the executor model (RefExec).
- S.ok includes the well-formedness of the store (for refRingStore, Pool.WF and a place id below the compiled place count), which the requirement does not state. It is the store interface's reading of 'holds a queue': a store that is not well formed holds no queue view reads faithfully, which is CONC-022's subject. The precompiled cycle keeps the pool well formed and its place count fixed on a compiled net (pcCycle_rel in Refinement), so on the reference every compiled place stays in S.ok at every state a run reaches from a well-formed start. Splitting ok into 'place known' and a separate well-formedness hypothesis would change the store interface CONC-022 is stated over, so the line uses S.ok as CONC-022 does.
- Places outside the store are not constrained (clash conc-b#8): every shipped precompiled executor also merges into the materialised marking the tokens it keeps for unknown places (rust/libpetri-runtime/src/precompiled_backend.rs:880-881 extra_marking, java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/runtime/PrecompiledNetExecutor.java:1587 extraTokens, typescript/src/runtime/precompiled-net-executor.ts:1767-1771 unknownPlaceTokens), which no ring holds. That retention is CORE-072's subject (AC3 there); the line neither requires nor forbids it on places outside the store. On a place the store holds a queue for it forbids it: a side marking seeded with the whole initial marking, known places included, hands those tokens out twice (CONC_025_forbids_seeded). The editorial rewording of AC3 that names those tokens waits for ruling D20.
- AC1 (normal execution cycles do not create or update a Marking object) is not encoded: whether an object is allocated or written is not observable in a state model, so AC1 is a quality criterion, shown by the test derivation (a run with a noop event store creates no Marking until the result is requested), which is not encoded either. That a token deposited on an unknown place updates the retained marking in a normal cycle (clash conc-b#8) is AC1's and waits for D20 with it. The Kind line is B, the kind of its one encoded line, following the one-letter convention of the signed blocks; the laziness of the title and AC1 are quality criteria with no line, and whether the Kind line changes for Q content is ruling D21, which is open.
- AC2 (the Marking is materialized on demand for event emission, debug or the result) is not encoded: when the executor materialises is the subject of the requirements that ask for a marking ([EVT-014], [EXEC-041], and the snapshot request of [ENV-014], which the body's list of occasions omits, clash conc-b#8). The line says what every materialisation returns, at whatever reachable state it is asked for.
- AC3 is the line. CONC_025_forbids_stale rejects an executor that materialises once and hands out that marking after later cycles (the hazard the TypeScript getMarking docstring names, typescript/src/runtime/precompiled-net-executor.ts:1778-1794; caching outside a run, which TypeScript does, is allowed, since no step runs between). CONC_025_forbids_blockOrder rejects one that reads each ring from the start of its block instead of from its head: it hands out the right tokens in the wrong order once a ring has wrapped, so 'accurately reflects' is read with queue order, as the EARS sentence says.

- ✗ **forbids** `Libpetri.Spec.CONC_025_forbids_blockOrder` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.CONC_025): ✗ An executor that reads its rings in block order violates CONC-025: at the start state the ring has not wrapped and it hands out `5, 6`, which is right; after one cycle the ring has wrapped, place `0`'s queue is `6, 7`, and it hands out `7, 6`.

- ✗ **forbids** `Libpetri.Spec.CONC_025_forbids_snapshot` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.CONC_025): ✗ An executor that materialises from a copy of its rings violates CONC-025: after one cycle the live ring of place `0` holds `6, 7`, and it still hands out `5, 6`.

- ✗ **forbids** `Libpetri.Spec.CONC_025_forbids_stale` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.CONC_025): ✗ An executor that materialises once violates CONC-025: from the start state, materialised as `5, 6`, one cycle moves place `0`'s queue to `6, 7`, and the executor still hands out `5, 6`.

<a id="Libpetri-Spec-CONC_026"></a>
## CONC-026: Optional output validation skip (option enabled)

`Libpetri.Spec.CONC_026` · Kind **N** · Scope an executor that offers the option, with the option enabled · Source **verbatim** (spec/05-concurrency.md) · Sign-off **pending** · Statement hash `03cde977bb7d7835`

| Natural language | Plain reading | Lean statement |
|---|---|---|
| *While* the option is enabled, the executor *shall* deposit the tokens an action wrote without validating them against the transition's output spec.<br><br>The skip covers the whole spec, its `Place` and `ForwardInput` leaves included: a transition whose output spec is a single leaf is not checked for a write to that place either.<br><br>While the option is enabled they do not apply: a firing that ends with its action deposits the action's write whether or not it equals an output branch.<br><br>The option skips nothing else.<br><br>A write to a place the transition does not declare as an output still fails ([CORE-063]).<br><br>The build-time checks of [IO-011], [IO-012], [IO-013] and [IO-014] run when the transition is built, before any executor exists, and no executor option reaches them.<br><br>When enabled, output tokens are deposited without validation. | 1. For every transition t that builds, whatever its output spec (an And, an Xor, or a single Place or ForwardInput leaf), every marking m at which t is enabled and every deposit d that writes only output places of t:<br>2. some firing of t from m deposits d.<br>3. Every firing of every transition deposits only in output places of the transition.<br>4. A transition that does not build never fires. | <pre>fun {N} [DecidableEq N] F ↦<br>  (∀ (t : Reference.Trans N),<br>      Builds t →<br>        ∀ (m : CountMarking N),<br>          Enabled t m →<br>            ∀ (d : List N),<br>              (∀ (p : N), Produced d p → OutputArc t p) → ∃ m', F t m d m') ∧<br>    (∀ (t : Reference.Trans N) (d : List N),<br>        on fun m m' ↦ F t m d m', shall fun x x_1 ↦<br>          ∀ (p : N), Produced d p → OutputArc t p) ∧<br>      ∀ (t : Reference.Trans N),<br>        ¬Builds t → ∀ (m : N → ℕ) (d : List N) (m' : N → ℕ), ¬F t m d m'</pre> |

**Assumptions**

- The model is the firing relation F of one executor that has the option and has it enabled, each firing read as one step from a marking to a marking (glossary: Fire, Deposit); timing and priority play no part. The action may write any tokens into the transition's output places, so 'deposit the tokens an action wrote without validating them' is read as: every such write is the deposit of some firing (the first two lines). Deposits are compared per place (CORE-036), so several tokens in one place are one more such write.
- 'The skip covers the whole spec, its Place and ForwardInput leaves included' is why the first line ranges over every output spec: a transition whose output spec is Place(P) also fires with a write that misses P (CONC_026_forbids_leafValidated).
- 'It also covers the join-relay check of [NU-054] and the multiplicity warning of [IO-016] AC4, both of which run as part of validation.': a correlation name and a diagnostic are below the token-count granularity of the firing semantics; not encoded.
- The paragraph naming IO-010, IO-011, IO-012, the per-firing check of IO-015 and the last two firing lines of CORE-036 is a scope: those blocks describe an executor with output validation enabled (their scope strings say so), and this block describes the executor with the option enabled. Theorem CONC_026_scoped shows both hold at once, each of its own executor, and that every firing of the validating executor on a transition that builds is a firing of the skipping one.
- 'The option skips nothing else' and 'A write to a place the transition does not declare as an output still fails ([CORE-063])' are the third line: a write outside the output places is not the deposit of any firing.
- 'A firing that ends with the timeout outcome deposits what [IO-013] and [IO-014] say.' is those blocks' subject, over the relation of timed-out firings; it is not restated here. A timeout deposit writes only output places, so the first line covers it.
- 'The build-time checks ... no executor option reaches them' is the fourth line: a transition that does not build (glossary: Builds) is not a transition any executor holds, so it never fires, the option enabled or not.
- The first sentence's MAY (whether an executor offers the option at all), 'for known-correct nets' and the performance sentence are not encoded: the block describes an executor that offers the option, with it enabled. The implementation notes are not normative.
- AC1 (the option is opt-in, validation is on by default) is about the builder's default, not about the firing relation; not encoded.
- AC2 (when enabled, output tokens are deposited without validation) is the first two lines.
- AC3 (when disabled, validation behaves identically to the bitmap executor) is the plain firing relation's subject (IO-010 to IO-015); not encoded here.
- AC4 (Place(P) writing nothing, And(A, B) writing only A, both deposited) is the first two lines; CONC_026_nonvacuous fires both under the witness.
- AC5 (no NU-054 diagnostic, no IO-016 AC4 warning) is below the token-count granularity; not encoded.
- AC6 (a write to an undeclared place still fails, and building a transition that IO-012 rejects still fails) is the third and fourth lines.

**Evidence**

- ✓ **holds** `Libpetri.Spec.CONC_026_skip` (Libpetri.Spec.Clashes): ✓ CONC-026 holds of the skip-validation firings (`refFireSkipValidation`).
  <pre>∀ {N : Type} [inst : DecidableEq N], CONC_026 refFireSkipValidation</pre>

<a id="Libpetri-Spec-CORE_002"></a>
## CORE-002: Place Identity

`Libpetri.Spec.CORE_002` · Kind **F** · Scope all implementations · Source **verbatim** (spec/01-core-model.md) · Sign-off **pending** · Statement hash `a45d3b0acc9038aa`

| Natural language | Plain reading | Lean statement |
|---|---|---|
| Two places that are the same place *shall* have the same name.<br><br>Two places with the same name and the same token type *shall* be the same place.<br><br>An implementation *shall* identify a place either by its name, so that two places with the same name are the same place, or by its name and its token type, so that two places that are the same place have the same token type. | 1. For every place model M (place objects with a name, a token type and a key; two objects are the same place when their keys are equal):<br>2. for all place objects p and q, if p and q are the same place, p and q have the same name;<br>3. for all place objects p and q, if p and q have the same name and the same token type, p and q are the same place;<br>4. either for all place objects p and q, if p and q have the same name, p and q are the same place; or for all place objects p and q, if p and q are the same place, p and q have the same token type. | <pre>fun {Nm Ty} M ↦<br>  (∀ (p q : M.P), M.Same p q → M.name p = M.name q) ∧<br>    (∀ (p q : M.P), M.name p = M.name q → M.ty p = M.ty q → M.Same p q) ∧<br>      ((∀ (p q : M.P), M.name p = M.name q → M.Same p q) ∨<br>        ∀ (p q : M.P), M.Same p q → M.ty p = M.ty q)</pre> |

**Assumptions**

- A place model (PlaceKeyed, Reference/Build.lean) is the place identity of one implementation: its place objects P, the name and the token type of each, and the key K the engine identifies a place object by. Two place objects are the same place exactly when their keys are equal (PlaceKeyed.Same). K is the place type N of every other block (glossary PlaceName N := N, identity = equality on N): refPlacesByName_K and refPlacesByNameType_K. 'The same way throughout the implementation' is that one implementation is one place model, with one key function; an implementation that mixes two identities is modelled by one key that does both, and line 2 rejects the mix TypeScript's builder has (CORE_002_forbids_tsBuilderMix). An implementation whose equality and hash of place objects disagree is outside the model: their agreement is the host language's contract, and today Rust's PartialEq and Hash both use the name alone (rust/libpetri-core/src/place.rs:50-62).
- AC1 (a place is the same place as itself) holds of every place model by construction: the same place is equality of keys, an equivalence (PlaceKeyed.same_equivalence). It is no line of the statement, and no model can break it.
- AC2 (two independently constructed places with different names are never the same place) is line 1, read backwards: places with different names are never the same place. A model in which every place is one place (CORE_002_forbids_onePlace) violates it, and so does identity by token type alone (CORE_002_mutant_noLine1_killed), which lines 2 and 3 accept.
- AC3 (place identity is stable across the lifetime of a net) holds by the type of the model: the key of a place object is a function of the object alone, with no state, net or time argument, so no model can change a place's identity during a run.
- Line 2 is the sentence ruling D82 (a) adds against the text before it, which allowed reference or ID-based equality, under which two place objects constructed separately with the same name and token type are two places; no implementation's engine does that (rust/libpetri-core/src/place.rs:50-62 compares names, java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/core/Place.java:23-26 is a record of name and token type, typescript/src/runtime/compiled-net.ts:85-102 keys places by name, and the Python binding identifies a place by its name, rust/libpetri-py/src/model.rs:39). Reference identity (core002_byRef) satisfies lines 1 and 3 (CORE_002_mutant_noLine2, killed by CORE_002_mutant_noLine2_killed) and violates line 2 (CORE_002_forbids_byRef).
- Line 3 is the rest of ruling D82 (a): the identity is one of the two that exist, the name or the name and the token type. With lines 1 and 2 it leaves exactly those two: under its first branch the same place is the same name, under its second the same place is the same name and token type. A key between the two, such as the name and a coarsening of the token type (core002_coarseType), meets lines 1 and 2 and fails line 3 (CORE_002_mutant_noLine3_killed). Name identity (TypeScript, Rust, Python; CORE_002_byName) takes the first branch and name-and-type identity (Java; CORE_002_byNameType) the second. They differ on two places of one name and different token types, one place by name and two by name and type (place_identity_divergence, cited by MOD-024).
- Which language uses which identity is not a line: the statement is over one abstract model and does not name a language. The body's per-language sentences are carried by the two witness models, whose definitions cite the runtime code (Reference/Build.lean, refPlacesByName and refPlacesByNameType). Java's token type is the run-time class a Java place records (Place.java:23-26, Class<T> tokenType), so the model's token type for Java is that class: Place<List<String>> and Place<List<Integer>> of one name have one token type and are one place, which is name-and-type identity, not an identity between the two.
- In TypeScript and Python the host language's own equality of place objects is not the place identity: place("A") in TypeScript returns a new object each time (typescript/src/core/place.ts:25-27), and a Python Place defines no equality, so two objects of one name are unequal objects and one place. The model reads a place object as its name and token type, so host object equality is not modelled. TypeScript's net builder keeps the places declared on it in a Set of objects (typescript/src/core/petri-net.ts:158 and :212-227) and the Set of IO-017's output places compares by reference too, while the compiled net keys places by name: that is a known TypeScript departure from this requirement ('the same way throughout the implementation', and line 2), recorded as a defect to fix by ruling D66 (a) under CORE-040 (RD-03 in spec/runtime-defects.md). Its model, core002_tsBuilderMix, is rejected (CORE_002_forbids_tsBuilderMix). CORE_002_byName is the witness of the identity of TypeScript's engine, the compiled net, not of the builder's place set.
- In Java two places of one name and different token types are two places, so a Java net may hold two places with one name. Requirements keyed by place name (snapshot and restore, CORE-073; event and export identifiers) assume one place per name in Java, the place analogue of the unique transition names of ruling D10; CORE-073 already puts such a net outside snapshot and restore. This block states no such assumption itself.
- The Note (a body place instantiated under two prefixes gives two distinct places) is MOD-010's renaming applied to the key: the two instances have different names, so line 1 makes them different places. A key that strips the prefix (core002_stripPrefix) makes "a/x" and "b/x" one place and is rejected (CORE_002_forbids_stripPrefix). Renaming itself is the composition model's (wave W8).
- The test derivation is lines 1 and 2 with CORE_002_nonvacuous: two places named A and B are different places (line 1); one place referenced twice, and two places constructed separately with one name and one token type, are one place (line 2, the place object (A, 0) the same as an equal one under both identities); and one name with token types 0 and 1 is one place by name (TypeScript, Rust, Python) and two by name and type (Java) (place_identity_divergence). That the engine holds one place of that name in the compiled net is CONC-007's line 1 over the places of the net.

**Evidence**

- ✓ **holds** `Libpetri.Spec.CORE_002_byName` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.CORE_002): ✓ Name identity (TypeScript, Rust, Python) satisfies CORE-002: the key is the name, and the name alone decides (line 3, first branch).
  <pre>∀ {Nm Ty : Type}, CORE_002 refPlacesByName</pre>
- ✓ **holds** `Libpetri.Spec.CORE_002_byNameType` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.CORE_002): ✓ Name-and-type identity (Java) satisfies CORE-002: the key is the pair, so the same place has one token type (line 3, second branch).
  <pre>∀ {Nm Ty : Type}, CORE_002 refPlacesByNameType</pre>
- ✗ **forbids** `Libpetri.Spec.CORE_002_forbids_byRef` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.CORE_002): ✗ Reference identity violates CORE-002 (line 2): the place objects constructed first and second, both named "A" with token type 0, are two places.
  <pre>¬CORE_002 core002_byRef</pre>
- ✗ **forbids** `Libpetri.Spec.CORE_002_forbids_onePlace` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.CORE_002): ✗ A model in which every place is one place violates CORE-002 (line 1, AC2): the places "A" and "B" are the same place with different names.
  <pre>¬CORE_002 core002_onePlace</pre>
- ✗ **forbids** `Libpetri.Spec.CORE_002_forbids_stripPrefix` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.CORE_002): ✗ A key that strips the composition prefix violates CORE-002 (line 1, the Note): "a/x" and "b/x" are one place with two names.
  <pre>¬CORE_002 core002_stripPrefix</pre>
- ✗ **forbids** `Libpetri.Spec.CORE_002_forbids_tsBuilderMix` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.CORE_002): ✗ TypeScript's builder place set mixed with name keys violates CORE-002 (line 2): a declared "A" (object 0) and an arc-only "A", both of token type 0, are two places.
  <pre>¬CORE_002 core002_tsBuilderMix</pre>
- ✗ **mutant** `Libpetri.Spec.CORE_002_mutant_noLine1_killed` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.CORE_002): Identity by token type alone kills the mutant: the same name and token type give the same token type, so the same place (line 2), and the same place has one token type (line 3), but the places "A" and "B" of one token type are one place with two names (line 1).
  <pre>CORE_002_mutant_noLine1 core002_byType ∧ ¬CORE_002 core002_byType</pre>
- ✗ **mutant** `Libpetri.Spec.CORE_002_mutant_noLine2_killed` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.CORE_002): Reference identity kills the mutant: each object's key is the object, so the same place has one name (line 1) and one token type (line 3), but two objects constructed separately with one name and one token type are two places (line 2).
  <pre>CORE_002_mutant_noLine2 core002_byRef ∧ ¬CORE_002 core002_byRef</pre>
- ✗ **mutant** `Libpetri.Spec.CORE_002_mutant_noLine3_killed` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.CORE_002): The coarsened key kills the mutant: the key carries the name (line 1) and is a function of the name and token type (line 2), but the places ("A", 0) and ("A", 1) of one name are two places, so the name alone does not decide, and ("A", 0) and ("A", 2) are one place with two token types (line 3).
  <pre>CORE_002_mutant_noLine3 core002_coarseType ∧ ¬CORE_002 core002_coarseType</pre>
- ✓ **nonvacuous** `Libpetri.Spec.CORE_002_nonvacuous` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.CORE_002): ✓ All three lines of CORE-002 are exercised by the references. Under name identity two place objects of one name are one place even with different token types (line 3, first branch), and places named "A" and "B" are different places (line 1); under name-and-type identity a place is the same place as an equal place object (line 2) and two places of one name and different token types are two places (line 3, second branch), so the two references differ.

<a id="Libpetri-Spec-CORE_003"></a>
## CORE-003: Place Type Safety

`Libpetri.Spec.CORE_003` · Kind **A** · Scope all executors · Source **verbatim** (spec/01-core-model.md) · Sign-off **pending** · Statement hash `10404e5f1c1a497a`

| Natural language | Plain reading | Lean statement |
|---|---|---|
| A place has a declared token type, and a token is compatible with a place when its value is of that type.<br><br>A token without a value, the unit token ([CORE-012]), is compatible with every place.<br><br>The engine does not check the type of a token it deposits or a host adds: the net's author and the host keep an action's outputs, a forwarded token ([IO-014]) and an injected token compatible with their places.<br><br>*When* a transition fires from a marking in which every token is compatible with its place, nothing else changes the marking between the firing's consumption and its deposit, and every token the firing deposits is compatible with the place it is deposited to, every token a place holds after the firing *shall* be compatible with that place.<br><br>*When* a transition fires from a marking in which every token is compatible with its place, every token its action receives from one of its input places or read places *shall* be compatible with that place.<br><br>*When* a transition can fire from a marking and deposit tokens to a list of places, it *shall* also be able to fire from that marking, delivering the same tokens to its action, and deposit to the same places, in the same order, any tokens compatible with them.<br><br>A firing whose action outputs a token with a compatible value to a place succeeds. | 1. For a net whose places have the declared types ty (a token is compatible with place p when every value val gives it is of type ty p by HasType; a token without a value is compatible with every place), every transition t with no input arc and read arc on one place (ruling D15), and every firing of t from M that delivers δ, deposits e and leaves M':<br>2. if every token of M is compatible with its place and every token of e is compatible with the place it is deposited to, every token of M' is compatible with its place;<br>3. if every token of M is compatible with its place, every token δ delivers as consumed from an input place p is compatible with p;<br>4. if every token of M is compatible with its place, every token δ delivers as read from a read place p is compatible with p;<br>5. for every deposit e' to the same places as e, in the same order, whose every token is compatible with its place, t also fires from M, delivering δ and depositing e'. | <pre>fun {N T Ty V} [DecidableEq N] ty val HasType Q ↦<br>  ∀ (t : Reference.Trans N),<br>    NoInputRead t →<br>      (∀ (δ : Delivered N T) (e : List (N × T)),<br>          on fun M M' ↦ Q t M δ e M', shall fun M M' ↦<br>            CompatibleMarking ty val HasType M →<br>              CompatibleDeposit ty val HasType e → CompatibleMarking ty val HasType M') ∧<br>        (∀ (δ : Delivered N T) (e : List (N × T)),<br>            on fun M M' ↦ Q t M δ e M', shall fun M x ↦<br>              CompatibleMarking ty val HasType M →<br>                ∀ p ∈ inPlaces t, ∀ x ∈ δ.inputs p, TokenCompatible ty val HasType p x) ∧<br>          (∀ (δ : Delivered N T) (e : List (N × T)),<br>              on fun M M' ↦ Q t M δ e M', shall fun M x ↦<br>                CompatibleMarking ty val HasType M →<br>                  ∀ (p : N),<br>                    ReadArc t p → ∀ x ∈ δ.reads p, TokenCompatible ty val HasType p x) ∧<br>            ∀ (δ : Delivered N T) (e e' : List (N × T)),<br>              on fun M M' ↦ Q t M δ e M', shall fun M x ↦<br>                List.map Prod.fst e' = List.map Prod.fst e →<br>                  CompatibleDeposit ty val HasType e' → ∃ M'', Q t M δ e' M''</pre> |

**Assumptions**

- A firing is one step Q t M δ e M' (glossary: QFireRel): t fires from the queue marking M, delivers δ to its action (the consumed tokens per input place and the read tokens per read place), deposits e (places and tokens, in deposit order; the glossary calls e what the action emits) and leaves M'. T is the token. The net's declared typing is three parameters of the statement, fixed for the net and not quantified inside it: ty p is the declared type of place p, val x the value of token x (none for a token without a value) and HasType τ v says that v is a value of type τ. The reference satisfies the block at every typing (CORE_003_reference).
- The typing is a parameter so that the block states type safety and not provenance. Read with every typing quantified inside the statement, the lines would also apply to a typing that gives every place its own type, and would then reject an engine that moves a deposited token between two places of one declared type; the prose allows that engine, and the block does too (CORE_003_allows_sameTypeMove), while the quantified reading rejects it (CORE_003_everyTyping_rejects_sameTypeMove). Provenance is CORE-010's subject.
- Ruling D36 (a). The first three quoted sentences define compatibility and say who keeps it; they are assumptions on the net's author and the host (kind A), not engine behaviour, and are encoded as TokenCompatible (sentences 1 and 2) and as the deposit premise of line 1 (sentence 3). Sentence 2 is the definition's none case (CORE_003_unit_compatible): a token whose projection is none carries no value to check and meets the deposit premise at any place. It is a definitional sentence; which tokens of T are unit tokens is fixed by val, and no theorem here ties the executor's unit token to it. Whether the deposit of the timeout outcome (IO-013) is a step of Q is the queue model's question (CORE-010's assumes: a timed-out completion is not); where it is, its unit tokens meet the premise of line 1 at every place. Java's Place.accepts reads a null value the same way.
- Sentence 3 is checked against the reference: the reference deposits whatever the firing deposits, an incompatible token included, so the reading of line 1 without its deposit premise is false of it (CORE_003_engine_unchecked, cited for the sentence). That premise is what the deposit's author owes: an action's emitted outputs (Rust's ctx.output takes a place name and a value of any type; TypeScript and Java type the handle only at compile time; Python checks nothing), a ForwardInput whose from and to places have different types (TypeScript and Rust accept such a pair), and a token a host injects or restores (a host step, not a step of Q). Who supplies such a token is outside the firing relation; the block does not show a ForwardInput separately, since in RefQFire a forwarded token is an entry of e like any output.
- The first EARS sentence is line 1. It is scoped, as CORE-010's first two sentences are, to a firing with nothing else changing the marking between its consumption and its deposit: an asynchronous action's outputs are deposited when its completion is processed, in a later cycle, and a host may inject a token in between. Each part keeps the invariant on its own (consumption removes tokens, a deposit of compatible tokens adds compatible ones), but the interleaved form is a property of the executor model (RefExec, W5), not of one step of Q; no block cited here covers it yet.
- The second EARS sentence is lines 2 and 3, split by arc kind so that δ.inputs is consulted only at input places and δ.reads only at read places. It is why an action's typed read of its input succeeds when the marking is compatible (Rust's input::<T> downcast, CORE-060). A correlated input of a match specification (NU-020) delivers tokens of its own place too, so the sentence needs no exception; Reference.Trans carries no match specification (ruling D30). What δ holds under a place that is neither an input nor a read place of t is not constrained, as in CORE-010's lines 4 and 5: the sentence speaks only of tokens received from input and read places, and an action asking for an undeclared input place is CORE-060 AC4's error case (RefCtx, W3).
- The third EARS sentence is line 4, and AC1 (a firing whose action outputs a token with a compatible value to a place succeeds) is line 4 with line 1: whatever tokens a firing deposits, the same firing with compatible tokens to the same places is a step too, and it keeps a compatible marking compatible. Line 4 kills an engine with a run-time type table that refuses a compatible deposit (CORE_003_forbids_refuseCompatible); lines 1 to 3 accept that engine, since it is a sub-relation of the reference (CORE_003_mutant_noLine4_killed_refuseCompatible). Line 4 asks nothing of an incompatible deposit: whether an engine may refuse one is not CORE-003's, and an engine that checks types at run time satisfies it.
- Every line is stated for transitions satisfying NoInputRead (ruling D15), as CORE-010's lines are: lines 1 to 3 are a corollary of CORE-010 (core003_lines123_of_CORE_010), line 1 from CORE-010 line 1 (every token after the firing was held by the place or deposited there) and lines 2 and 3 from CORE-010 lines 4 and 5 (every delivered token was held by its place). A transition with an input arc and a read arc on one place is rejected when it is built (EXEC-012) and never fires, so the EARS sentences, which carry no such premise, say nothing more than the lines about a transition that can fire.
- Each of lines 1 to 3 has a firing relation that breaks it from a compatible marking with a compatible deposit: an engine that puts a deposited token in a place of another type than the one it is deposited to (CORE_003_forbids_misroute, line 1), and an action handed an input token (CORE_003_forbids_inputElsewhere, line 2) or a read token (CORE_003_forbids_readElsewhere, line 3) taken from a place of another type. The deposit premise of line 1 is load-bearing in the other direction: the reading without it is stronger and false of the reference (CORE_003_engine_unchecked), so no relation separates it from line 1 as a mutant would.
- Like most on … shall lines, lines 1 to 3 hold of the relation that takes no step; line 4 does too, since it only extends steps Q takes. The coverage conjunct QCovers Q F of the queue consistency theorem rules out the empty relation, as for CORE-010.
- The fourth and fifth sentences of the description and AC2 are not encoded. The fourth (an implementation that keeps a run-time token type for each place rejects an initial marking that puts a token with an incompatible value in a place) and AC2 are Java's Marking.from check, run when either Java executor is built. The initial marking is CORE-072's Init, over token counts, so no step relation here sees the token's value: the check is tested, not encoded (kind Q), and it is not part of the block's scope. Java does not check later deposits (Marking.addToken, ctx.output) at run time. The fifth (a compiler rejects a token of another type where an API call takes a typed place handle) is API shape: compile-time typing is not claimed (ruling D36 (a)), and whether the typed API surfaces bind the Python binding is open ruling D99 and is not relied on.
- The test derivation (a transition outputs an integer token to an Integer place and succeeds; in Java an initial marking with a string token is rejected) is AC1 and AC2; CORE_003_nonvacuous fires the reference with the compatible deposit of 30 to place 2.

<a id="Libpetri-Spec-CORE_010"></a>
## CORE-010: Token Immutability

`Libpetri.Spec.CORE_010` · Kind **B** · Scope all executors · Source **verbatim** (spec/01-core-model.md) · Sign-off **pending** · Statement hash `e5baab372e4f3277`

| Natural language | Plain reading | Lean statement |
|---|---|---|
| A token is an immutable value object consisting of a typed payload value and a creation timestamp.<br><br>Once created, neither the value nor the timestamp can be modified.<br><br>*When* a transition fires and nothing else changes the marking between the firing's consumption and its deposit, every token a place holds after the firing *shall* be a token the place held before the firing, with the same value and creation timestamp, or a token the action emitted to that place, and the firing *shall* not duplicate any of these tokens.<br><br>*When* a transition fires and nothing else changes the marking between the firing's consumption and its deposit, every token that a place without a reset arc of the transition held before the firing *shall* still be in that place after the firing, with the same value and creation timestamp, unless the action received it from that place as a consumed input.<br><br>*When* a transition fires, every token its action receives from one of its input places or read places *shall* be a token that place held before the firing, with the same value and creation timestamp, and the action *shall* not receive a consumed token more often than its input place held it. | 1. For every transition t with no input arc and read arc on one place (ruling D15), every firing of t from M that delivers δ, emits e and leaves M':<br>2. every place p ends holding a sub-multiset of its tokens in M followed by the tokens e sends to p;<br>3. every place p that is neither an input place nor a reset place of t still holds every token it held in M, with multiplicity;<br>4. every input place p of t that is not a reset place holds every token it held in M, with multiplicity, apart from the tokens δ delivers as consumed from p;<br>5. the tokens δ delivers as consumed from an input place p are a sub-multiset of the tokens p held in M;<br>6. every token δ delivers as read from a read place p is a token p held in M. | <pre>fun {N T} [DecidableEq N] Q ↦<br>  ∀ (t : Reference.Trans N),<br>    NoInputRead t →<br>      (∀ (δ : Delivered N T) (e : List (N × T)),<br>          on fun M M' ↦ Q t M δ e M', shall fun M M' ↦<br>            ∀ (p : N), (M' p).Subperm (M p ++ EmittedTo e p)) ∧<br>        (∀ (δ : Delivered N T) (e : List (N × T)),<br>            on fun M M' ↦ Q t M δ e M', shall fun M M' ↦<br>              ∀ p ∉ inPlaces t, ¬ResetArc t p → (M p).Subperm (M' p)) ∧<br>          (∀ (δ : Delivered N T) (e : List (N × T)),<br>              on fun M M' ↦ Q t M δ e M', shall fun M M' ↦<br>                ∀ p ∈ inPlaces t, ¬ResetArc t p → (M p).Subperm (δ.inputs p ++ M' p)) ∧<br>            (∀ (δ : Delivered N T) (e : List (N × T)),<br>                on fun M M' ↦ Q t M δ e M', shall fun M x ↦<br>                  ∀ p ∈ inPlaces t, (δ.inputs p).Subperm (M p)) ∧<br>              ∀ (δ : Delivered N T) (e : List (N × T)),<br>                on fun M M' ↦ Q t M δ e M', shall fun M x ↦<br>                  ∀ (p : N), ReadArc t p → ∀ x ∈ δ.reads p, x ∈ M p</pre> |

**Assumptions**

- A firing is one step Q t M δ e M' (glossary: QFireRel): t fires from the queue marking M, delivers δ to its action (the consumed tokens per input place and the read tokens per read place), the action emits e (places and tokens, in emission order) and the firing leaves M'. T is the token itself, its value and its creation timestamp together, so 'the same value and creation timestamp' is equality in T, 'a token the place held' is membership in the place's queue and 'duplicate' or 'more often' compares occurrence counts (List.Subperm: every token occurs at most as often on the left as on the right).
- The firing is atomic, as one step of Q is: the first two EARS sentences are scoped to a firing with nothing else changing the marking between its consumption and its deposit. In all three runtimes an asynchronous action's outputs are deposited when its completion is processed, in a later cycle than the consumption (Java BitmapNetExecutor fireTransition and its completion handler; Rust and TypeScript alike), and other firings and injected tokens can change the marking in between, so after such a firing a place need not hold the tokens it held when the firing consumed. The third EARS sentence is local to the consumption and needs no scope. The same property for interleaved firings (each firing takes the head of its input places when it starts and appends at the tail when it completes) is stated locally by EXEC-010 and EXEC-020; over the executor cycle it is the companion of the executor model (RefExec, W5).
- The first quoted sentence is the definition the statement is read against: a token is its value and its creation timestamp, compared by content (a value object), which is equality in T. The 'typed payload' (a value of the place's token type) is CORE-001's and IO-006's subject and is not encoded; T is one abstract type for every place.
- The second quoted sentence is read at the engine seam, as the three EARS sentences restate it: the engine never rewrites, drops or copies a token it holds or moves. The same property at other seams belongs to their IDs: a Forward keeps the consumed token's value and timestamp (IO-014 AC5, below RefQFire), a restore keeps both (CORE-073 AC1), and tokens an action publishes before it completes (IO-015) are deposited outside a single firing (RefExec, Phase 2). An action or user code mutating a token object, deep immutability of the payload (a Java record holding a mutable object, a Rust Arc<T> with interior mutability) and runtime freezing in TypeScript are API shape (AC3), not claimed here.
- e is the emission of a completion the executor processed and output validation accepted ([EXEC-020], [EXEC-021], ruling D17); a discarded, timed-out, stopped or failed completion is not a step of Q. The tokens of e are new tokens the action created, so the block says nothing about their values or timestamps (CORE-011's subject). Because e is a parameter of the step, line 1 alone accepts a relation that re-stamps a place's tokens and lists the new copies in e; lines 2 and 3 kill it whatever e lists, since the original tokens must still be there (CORE_010_forbids_launder).
- Every line is stated for transitions satisfying NoInputRead (ruling D15): a transition with an input arc and a read arc on one place is rejected when it is built (EXEC-012) and never fires, so the EARS sentences, which carry no such premise, say nothing more than the lines about any transition that can fire. The reference meets the lines without that premise too; the premise is there so that the block is exactly a corollary of the signed EXEC blocks, which carry it.
- Derived: under D15, the lines follow from EXEC-020 (every place keeps a base followed by its emitted tokens; a place without an input arc and a reset arc keeps its queue as base, an input place that is not a reset place a sublist of it), EXEC-013 line 1 (a reset place holds exactly its emitted tokens), EXEC-010 line 1 (an input place that is not a reset place ends as a permutation of its queue after the consumed prefix followed by its emitted tokens), EXEC-010 line 2 (the delivered inputs are the FIFO prefix) and EXEC-012 line 1 (every read token is the head of the place), by CORE_010_of_EXEC. Every relation the forbids theorems here reject is therefore also rejected by one of those blocks; the block adds the link from the CORE-010 prose, not a new constraint.
- Line 1 is the first EARS sentence. A firing that re-stamps the tokens a place keeps onto pairs the place did not hold is killed by it (CORE_010_forbids_restamp; lines 2 and 3 kill it too). A firing that keeps every token and adds one more copy of a kept token is killed by line 1 alone (CORE_010_forbids_dup): lines 2 and 3 ask only that the held tokens stay, so its 'shall not duplicate' half is line 1's, and a reading of line 1 by membership accepts the copy (CORE_010_mutant_line1Membership_killed_dup). Order is not compared: that the kept tokens are the queue after the consumed prefix, in order, is EXEC-010's and EXEC-020's.
- Lines 2 and 3 are the second EARS sentence, split by whether the place is an input place, so that δ.inputs is consulted only where t has an input arc. They catch a rewrite that line 1 cannot see because the new token equals another held or emitted token: unit tokens (CORE-012) whose value ring and timestamp ring run out of step (CORE_010_forbids_desync, line 3), a place that stamps every token with its last arrival so that a held token becomes a copy of the emitted one (CORE_010_forbids_lastArrival, line 2), and the laundering relation above (CORE_010_forbids_launder, line 2).
- Lines 4 and 5 are the third EARS sentence, split by arc kind: line 4 for input places, line 5 for read places. An altered copy handed over as an input (CORE_010_forbids_alteredInput) or as a read (CORE_010_forbids_alteredRead) is killed, and so is an action that receives the head token k times for an exactly(k) input (CORE_010_forbids_headTwice, line 4). Line 5 is membership only: a read arc delivers the head once per arc, so a place read by two arcs legitimately hands over one token twice (qReadsBag); the read multiplicity is EXEC-012's. Both lines are restricted to the input places and the read places of t: what an action receives from a place that is neither is not constrained here, as in EXEC-010 and EXEC-013, because the spec has no shall sentence on it.
- 'neither the value nor the timestamp': a reading under which only the value is immutable accepts a firing that keeps every value and re-stamps the kept tokens; CORE-010 kills it (CORE_010_mutant_valueOnly_killed). A reading by membership instead of multiplicity accepts the laundering, desync, last-arrival and head-twice relations; CORE-010 kills each (CORE_010_mutant_membership_killed_*).
- Like most on … shall lines, the lines hold of the relation that takes no step; the coverage conjunct QCovers Q F of the queue consistency theorem rules that out (exec020_empty_not_covers).
- AC1 (token value accessible after creation and matching the original) is read at the engine seam as lines 1 to 5: a token the action receives, or a place keeps, is the token as created, value included (CORE_010_nonvacuous: the action receives (10, 0) and (20, 3), place 0 keeps (11, 1) and (12, 2), place 2 keeps (40, 5)). The accessor itself is API shape, checked by tests, not encoded.
- AC2 (token timestamp accessible after creation) is API shape: an accessor exists in every language with a token object. It is checked by tests and not encoded; that the timestamp a kept or delivered token carries is its original one is lines 1 to 5.
- AC3 (no API to mutate token fields after creation) is API shape (kind Q in the plan): checked by tests and by each language's type system, not encoded. Whether the API-shape criteria bind the Python binding, which has no token object, is open ruling D99 and is not relied on.
- The test derivation (create a token with value 42, its value is 42 and its timestamp is set) is AC1 and AC2 and is not encoded.

**Evidence**

- ✓ **holds** `Libpetri.Spec.CORE_010_reference` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.CORE_010): The reference queue firing satisfies CORE-010, as the corollary of the reference's EXEC-010, EXEC-012, EXEC-013 and EXEC-020 evidence (`CORE_010_of_EXEC`): a place ends holding its queue after the consume step (empty for a reset place, the queue after the delivered FIFO prefix otherwise) followed by the tokens emitted to it, and the read bag holds heads of the queue. The `ToString` instance only names the build check of EXEC-012 and does not occur in CORE-010.

<a id="Libpetri-Spec-CORE_011"></a>
## CORE-011: Token Creation

`Libpetri.Spec.CORE_011` · Kind **F** · Scope the host token factories of Java, TypeScript and Rust · Source **verbatim** (spec/01-core-model.md) · Sign-off **pending** · Statement hash `4bf10d2e3a4e2551`

| Natural language | Plain reading | Lean statement |
|---|---|---|
| *When* a host creates a token from a value through the default factory, the token *shall* hold that value and carry the reading of the host's wall clock at the call as its creation timestamp, whatever clock an executor runs on ([TIME-015]).<br><br>*When* a host creates a token from a value and a timestamp through the explicit-timestamp factory, the token *shall* hold that value and carry that timestamp, whatever the clocks read at the call.<br><br>*When* a host creates the canonical unit token, the token *shall* hold no value and carry the timestamp 0, whatever the clocks read at the call. | 1. For the token factory K (make the default factory, makeAt the explicit-timestamp factory, unit the canonical unit-token constructor, each called when the host's wall clock reads r.wall and an executor's epoch clock reads r.epoch, timestamps being integers):<br>2. for all readings r and every value v, the default factory's token holds v and carries the timestamp r.wall;<br>3. for all readings r, every timestamp s (negative ones included) and every value v, the explicit-timestamp factory's token holds v and carries the timestamp s;<br>4. for all readings r, the canonical unit token is a unit token (it holds no value) and carries the timestamp 0. | <pre>fun {V} K ↦<br>  (∀ (r : ClockReadings) (v : V), K.make r v = { val := some v, stamp := r.wall }) ∧<br>    (∀ (r : ClockReadings) (s : ℤ) (v : V),<br>        K.makeAt r s v = { val := some v, stamp := s }) ∧<br>      ∀ (r : ClockReadings), IsUnitToken FacTok.val (K.unit r) ∧ (K.unit r).stamp = 0</pre> |

**Assumptions**

- The model is a token factory K : TokenFactory V (block-local): three functions a host calls, the default factory make, the explicit-timestamp factory makeAt and the canonical unit-token constructor unit. Each takes the readings at the call (ClockReadings): wall, of the host's wall clock, and epoch, of the epoch clock of an executor the host runs, which differs from wall when that executor runs on an injected clock (TIME-015). A token (FacTok V) is an optional value, none for a token without a value (glossary: Unit token, IsUnitToken; CORE-012), and a timestamp. The model takes the readings as given: which reading a call sees, and the clocks themselves, are not modelled. The witness is refTokenFactory, and CORE-011 holds of no other factory (core011_unique).
- A timestamp is an integer count of the implementation's unit since the start of the epoch, negative before it: nanoseconds for a Java Instant, milliseconds in Rust, and for TypeScript a unit fine enough that the number given is a whole count of it (every finite number is a whole count of 2 to the power -1074). So a timestamp before the epoch, or finer than a millisecond, is in scope. Rust's timestamp is a u64, so its explicit-timestamp factory takes only s at least 0, and line 2 applies to those.
- A factory with state (a cache, a high-water mark) is read as the family of its states: CORE-011 holds of it when it holds at every state a host can reach. A default factory that clamps its stamp to the last stamp it handed out, so that AC2 holds while the wall clock goes back, violates line 1 at the state it reaches after a call at the wall reading 10 (CORE_011_forbids_clamp: called next at the wall reading 5, it stamps 10).
- Line 1 is the first sentence (ruling D64 (a)). 'The reading of the host's wall clock at the call' is r.wall; 'whatever clock an executor runs on' is that the stamp does not depend on r.epoch: the factory is called from host code, which no executor's clock reaches (core011_make_epoch_blind). A factory that always stamps 0 (CORE_011_forbids_zero), one that stamps a later reading (CORE_011_forbids_later) and one that stamps the epoch clock (CORE_011_mutant_epochClock_killed) violate it. The later reading stands in for any reading other than the one at the call: a test cannot see when inside the call the clock is read, so it checks that the stamp lies between wall readings taken just before and just after the call (core011_make_between).
- Line 2 is the second sentence: the explicit-timestamp construction TIME-015 requires (spec/03-timing.md, token stamping boundary), and what a snapshot restore (CORE-073) and a seed token (a seed-token helper is this factory applied to a clock's reading) use. A factory that re-stamps the given timestamp with the wall clock violates it (CORE_011_mutant_noExplicit_killed: the text before D64, with one factory, held of it). So do a factory that clamps a timestamp before the epoch to 0 (CORE_011_mutant_nonnegStamps_killed: the reading over non-negative timestamps only held of it) and one that rounds a timestamp to a coarser unit, as a Java Instant truncated to milliseconds (CORE_011_forbids_truncate).
- Line 3 is the third sentence (ruling D64 (a): stamp 0 only for the canonical unit constructor). That the canonical unit token is shared (a cached singleton in Java and TypeScript) and recognised by identity there, and how a runtime tells a unit token from a token holding a value, are CORE-012's and not modelled. A unit token the executor creates on a timeout outcome is not this constructor's: it is stamped from the epoch clock, which is the executor line. A unit constructor that stamps the wall clock (ruling D64 (b)) violates line 3 (CORE_011_mutant_unitUnspecified_killed: the reading with the unit token's timestamp left open held of it).
- AC1 (creating a token through the default factory yields a token that holds the given value and records the current reading of the host's wall clock) is line 1.
- AC2 (while the host's wall clock does not go back, two tokens created one after the other through the default factory have non-decreasing timestamps) is core011_monotone, derived from line 1 under the kind A assumption that the wall clock does not go back between the two calls (r1.wall ≤ r2.wall). Without it AC2 has no basis (clash K6): a wall clock may be set back, and then the second stamp is the lower one (core011_wall_back). AC2 does not hold of a default-factory token followed by an explicit-timestamp or a unit token, and the old AC2 alone does not pin the stamp (CORE_011_mutant_monotoneOnly_killed).
- AC3 (a token created at an explicit timestamp holds the given value and carries that timestamp unchanged, also before the epoch or finer than a millisecond where the timestamp type holds it) is line 2.
- AC4 (the canonical unit token holds no value and carries the timestamp 0) is line 3.
- AC5 (while an executor runs on an injected clock, a token created through the default factory carries the reading of the host's wall clock, not the injected clock's) is line 1 at readings whose epoch differs from wall: core011_make_epoch_blind, and CORE_011_mutant_epochClock_killed at a wall reading of 5 while the injected clock reads 100.
- The test derivation (a default token between two wall readings; two default tokens in sequence, the second timestamp at least the first; the same under an injected clock; tokens at explicit timestamps before the epoch and finer than a millisecond; the unit token; each holding its value) is CORE_011_nonvacuous on refTokenFactory, at wall readings 5 then 8 while an executor's injected epoch clock reads 100, with explicit timestamps -3 and 1500.
- Deferred to CORE-011's second block (wave W11, ruling D64 (a)): a token the executor creates (an action output written as a value, a token injected as a raw value, the unit token of a timeout outcome) carries a reading of the executor's epoch clock taken while the firing is in flight, and a forwarded token keeps its timestamp (IO-014). A token an action builds itself through a factory and outputs as a token (Java's output(Place, Token), TypeScript's outputToken) keeps that factory's stamp, which lines 1 and 2 already fix. CORE-035 AC2 and TIME-015 AC13 cite that line. It needs the executor model (RefExec) with an epoch clock next to the firing clock.
- Python has no token object and no token factory: a Python host passes values, and the Rust runtime it binds creates their tokens (ruling R5). Immutability of the token is CORE-010's.
